items.title: Merge vs rebase
items.context: git merge joins histories with a merge commit and rewrites nothing. git rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history but new commit IDs. Golden rule: don't rebase commits other people already have.

questions.prompt: Your feature branch is pushed and a teammate built on it. To pick up main's changes you should:
choices: Rebase and force-push without telling anyone
Delete the branch and start over
Merge main into it (or coordinate before rebasing)
questions.explanation: Rebasing a shared branch rewrites the history their work is based on.

items.title: Revert vs reset
items.context: git revert <sha> adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one — safe on shared branches. git reset moves the branch pointer back (--soft keeps changes staged, --hard discards them), rewriting history; only use it on local, unpushed work.

questions.prompt: A bad commit is already on main and deployed. The safe way to undo it is:
choices: git revert <sha> and push the new commit
git checkout an old tag on main
questions.explanation: Revert keeps history intact for everyone who has already pulled.

items.title: Delivery vs deployment
items.context: Continuous integration: merge small changes often, each verified by an automated build and tests. Continuous delivery: every change that passes is releasable, with a manual approval to production. Continuous deployment: it goes to production automatically.

questions.prompt: What separates continuous deployment from continuous delivery?
choices: Production releases happen automatically, without a manual approval
questions.explanation: Both keep main always releasable; deployment removes the human gate.

items.title: Build once, promote
items.context: Build the artifact (JAR, container image) once, tag it with the commit SHA, and promote that exact artifact through dev → staging → prod, changing only configuration. Rebuilding per environment risks shipping something you never tested.

questions.prompt: Why not rebuild the image separately for staging and production?
choices: The production build could differ from what was tested (new base image, dependency drift)
questions.explanation: Promote one immutable artifact; inject environment differences via config and secrets.

items.title: GitHub Actions basics
items.context: Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/. on: defines triggers (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch). Jobs run in parallel on fresh runners unless one declares needs: on another; steps in a job run in order.

questions.prompt: How do you make a deploy job wait for the test job?
choices: Put deploy first in the file
needs: test on the deploy job
questions.explanation: Without needs, jobs start at the same time.

items.title: CI caching
items.context: Cache dependency directories (~/.m2, ~/.npm) between runs with a key derived from the lockfile hash — e.g. hashFiles('**/package-lock.json'). The cache is reused until dependencies change, and a new key is created when they do.

questions.prompt: What should a dependency cache key be based on?
questions.explanation: Same lockfile → same dependencies → safe to reuse; a changed lockfile invalidates the cache.

items.title: Deployment strategies
items.context: Rolling: replace instances a few at a time. Blue-green: run the new version beside the old one and switch all traffic at once, so rollback is just switching back. Canary: send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp up.

questions.prompt: Which strategy gives the fastest rollback by flipping traffic back to the untouched old environment?
questions.explanation: The old (blue) environment keeps running until you're confident in green.

questions.prompt: You want to test a risky release on 5% of real users first. Use:
questions.explanation: Canaries limit the blast radius while real traffic validates the release.

items.title: Semantic versioning
items.context: SemVer is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. ^1.4.2 in npm accepts any 1.x.x at or above 1.4.2.

questions.prompt: You remove a public API endpoint from version 2.7.3. The next version is:
questions.explanation: Removing something clients use is a breaking change → major bump.

items.title: git stash
items.context: git stash shelves uncommitted changes and gives you a clean working tree; git stash pop reapplies the latest stash and drops it. git stash -u includes untracked files.

questions.prompt: You need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit. Use:
choices: git stash, switch, then git stash pop later
questions.explanation: Stashes are local and easy to forget — git stash list shows them.

items.title: cherry-pick
items.context: git cherry-pick <sha> applies one commit's changes on top of the current branch as a new commit — handy for backporting a fix to a release branch.

questions.prompt: A hotfix landed on main and must go to release/2.4 too. Use:
choices: Merge all of main into release/2.4
questions.explanation: Only that change moves, not everything else on main.

items.title: git bisect
items.context: git bisect binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a bug: mark one good and one bad commit, test the midpoint, repeat. git bisect run <script> automates it with a test script.

questions.prompt: A regression appeared somewhere in 500 commits. git bisect finds it in about:

items.title: .gitignore and tracked files
items.context: .gitignore only affects untracked files. If a file is already committed, adding it to .gitignore does nothing until you stop tracking it with git rm --cached <file> (which keeps your local copy).

questions.prompt: You added .env to .gitignore but Git still shows changes to it. Fix:
choices: git rm --cached .env and commit (and rotate any secrets it held)
questions.explanation: If it ever held secrets, they're in history: rotate them.

items.title: Branch protection
items.context: Protect main: require pull requests, passing status checks (build, tests, scans) and at least one approval; block force pushes and branch deletion.

questions.prompt: How do you ensure nobody merges to main with failing tests?
choices: Branch protection with required status checks
questions.explanation: CI becomes a gate, not a suggestion.

items.title: Feature flags
items.context: Feature flags decouple deploying code from releasing a feature: ship code turned off, enable it for internal users or a percentage of users, and turn it off instantly without a redeploy. Remove stale flags so they don't pile up.

choices: Turning a feature on or off without redeploying
questions.explanation: They enable trunk-based development with unfinished work merged but hidden.

items.title: Artifact repositories
items.context: Build outputs are stored in artifact repositories: container registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, Harbor) and package repositories (Nexus, Artifactory, Maven Central). Deploys pull a versioned artifact instead of rebuilding from source.

questions.prompt: Where should CI push the container image it built?
choices: A container registry such as ECR, GHCR or Harbor
questions.explanation: Tag it with the commit SHA (and a version) for traceability.

items.title: Pipeline as code
items.context: Defining the pipeline in the repository (Jenkinsfile, .gitlab-ci.yml, GitHub Actions YAML) versions it with the code, reviews changes in pull requests, and lets every branch carry its own pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why keep the pipeline definition in the repository?
choices: It's versioned and reviewed together with the code it builds
CI servers require it to be secret
questions.explanation: Clicking pipelines together in a UI isn't reproducible.

items.title: Flaky tests
items.context: A flaky test passes and fails without code changes (timing, ordering, shared state, the network). Automatic retries hide real failures and erode trust in CI. Track flaky tests, quarantine them if needed, and fix the root cause.

questions.prompt: The best long-term response to a flaky test is:
choices: Find and fix its non-determinism (quarantine it meanwhile)
questions.explanation: If people learn to ignore red builds, real bugs slip through.
